section: 4.4 Linking experiments to their artifacts
text:
4.4 Linking experiments to their artifacts
Production traces preserve what happened for real users. Research changes prompts, data, code, and models repeatedly, so comparable results retain their lineage. A run record keeps small metadata separate from large artifacts and links aggregate metrics to raw predictions.
Experiment run. one execution with immutable input identities, parameters, environment, outputs, and measured results.
MLflow, W&B, and similar systems store configurations, metrics, logs, and artifact references. Dataset tools such as DVC identify large data versions. The tracking server is not a substitute for source control or object storage: it links those systems so a chart point can be reproduced.
A comparison-ready run contains:

Question: the hypothesis or change being tested.
Inputs: source revision, dataset/evaluation-suite version, base model, prompt, and environment.
Execution: hardware, seed, parameters, start/end time, and failure/retry history.
Outputs: checkpoint or serving bundle, raw model responses, evaluator verdicts, and derived tables.
Metrics: aggregate values plus slice definitions, confidence or variance, and cost/latency.
Decision: whether to promote, reject, rerun, or investigate, with the responsible reviewer.







Figure 4.6: Experiment tracking joins parameters and measurements to the artifacts that make a run reproducible.



The following abbreviated MLflow example assumes that evaluate returns row-level verdict and timing records. The helper functions derive a results table and aggregate metrics from those records; they do not call a second evaluation with different inputs.

Code example: Experiment run with immutable inputs, aggregate measurements, and raw verdict evidence.


with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_params({
        "model_version": model_version,
        "prompt_version": prompt_version,
        "dataset_version": dataset_version,
        "temperature": temperature,
    })
    verdicts = evaluate(cases, judge)
    verdict_frame = to_table(verdicts)
    verdict_frame.to_parquet("raw_verdicts.parquet", index=False)
    mlflow.log_metrics({
        "accuracy": accuracy(verdicts),
        "consistent_rows": consistency(verdicts),
        "p95_latency_ms": p95_latency(verdicts),
    })
    mlflow.log_artifact("raw_verdicts.parquet")

Code walkthrough
Run identity: start_run creates one traceable experiment identity.
Input identity: Model, prompt, dataset, and temperature parameters define the evaluator configuration being compared.
Derived measurements: Accuracy, consistency, and p95 latency summarize different quality and operating dimensions from the same verdict set.
Raw evidence: raw_verdicts.parquet preserves row-level outputs needed to reproduce slices, disagreements, and aggregate metrics.
Result: A chart point remains auditable because its configuration and contributing row-level evidence share one run identity.
Limits: Production records also include source revision, environment or image digest, evaluator version, case count, failure count, and artifact checksum.

section: 4.5 Quality evaluation with LLM-as-a-judge
text:
4.5 Quality evaluation with LLM-as-a-judge
Experiment tracking can preserve any metric faithfully. It cannot repair a metric whose target, labels, or decision rules are ambiguous. Observed failures and a label definition lead to smaller measurable quality decisions.






Figure 4.7: A usable evaluator starts from real outputs, explicit bad/good criteria, and small metrics.



Observed outputs provide the starting point. A concrete disqualifying failure and a concrete desired property make the quality gap measurable. Smaller metrics separate factuality, relevance, style, safety, and task completion, which a broad question such as ‘is this answer good?’ mixes into one unstable judgment.






Figure 4.8: Evaluator design balances complexity, context, accuracy, consistency, and efficiency.



Evaluator design balances complexity, context, accuracy, consistency, and efficiency. More context can improve evidence coverage but degrade long-context reasoning and increase latency. A powerful judge may improve difficult cases but make the evaluation too expensive to run on every experiment. Decomposition makes each decision smaller and its failure easier to diagnose.
Ground truth. the reference label or outcome treated as correct for evaluation, together with its annotation rules and source record.
Ground-truth calibration precedes judge calibration. Annotator disagreements, ambiguous cases, label errors, and policy gaps reveal problems in the reference set. A judge that disagrees with an incorrect label is not adjusted to imitate the mistake.

Rubric-to-verdict trace
Rubric: label unsupported when any answer claim is absent from or contradicted by the supplied context; otherwise label supported. Return {label, claim, evidence_span, reason}.
Case: the answer says the contract renews in June, while the supplied context says July. The schema-valid verdict is unsupported, names the June claim, cites the July evidence span, and explains the contradiction.
Calibration compares this structured verdict with adjudicated labels. Parse validity, label agreement, and evidence-span correctness are measured separately so a syntactically valid but poorly supported verdict does not pass silently.

\[
\mathrm{Accuracy} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}}
\tag{4.1}\]
For this detector, the positive condition is an unsupported answer. A true positive (TP) is an unsupported answer correctly flagged; a false negative (FN) is an unsupported answer missed. A true negative (TN) is a supported answer accepted, and a false positive (FP) is a supported answer incorrectly flagged. Accuracy counts correct decisions among all cases. Precision, \(\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})\), asks how many flags are justified; recall, \(\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})\), asks how many unsupported answers are found.
\[
\mathrm{F1} = \frac{2 \cdot \mathrm{Precision} \cdot \mathrm{Recall}}{\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}
\tag{4.2}\]
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so a low value in either limits the combined score. A zero denominator means the corresponding rate is undefined for that sample; the report records the case count and its chosen undefined-value policy rather than silently treating it as a measured zero.

Worked calculation: hallucination-detector metrics
Confusion counts: Across 20 cases: TP = 7, TN = 9, FP = 1, FN = 3.
Accuracy: (7 + 9) ÷ 20 = 0.80.
Precision: 7 ÷ (7 + 1) = 0.875.
Recall: 7 ÷ (7 + 3) = 0.70.
F1: 2 × 0.875 × 0.70 ÷ (0.875 + 0.70) \(\approx\) 0.778.
Conclusion: The same 80% accuracy contains a recall problem that matters if missed hallucinations are costly.

section: 4.6 Checking evaluator consistency and agreement
text:
4.6 Checking evaluator consistency and agreement
Accuracy compares one set of verdicts with reference labels. An LLM judge can produce different verdicts for the same input, so one run may conceal an unstable verdict. Repeated runs reveal this variation, while accuracy measures correctness against the reference.
Consistency. the stability of an evaluator’s verdict across repeated runs of an unchanged case and configuration.
\[
C_i = \frac{\max_y \sum_{r=1}^{R} 1\left[\hat{y}_{i,r}=y\right]}{R}
\tag{4.3}\]
For case \(i\), \(\hat y_{i,r}\) is the label from repeat \(r\), and \(R\) is the number of repeats. The indicator is 1 when the label equals candidate label \(y\) and 0 otherwise. Summing counts that label’s votes; taking the maximum selects the modal count. Dividing by \(R\) gives the modal proportion \(C_i\). Averaging these proportions over cases differs from the full-agreement rate, which counts only cases where all \(R\) verdicts match.

Worked calculation: five votes on one evaluator case
Votes: good, bad, good, good, bad.
Modal label: good appears three times.
Consistency: 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60.
Correctness: If the reference label is good, the majority is correct but the case remains unstable.
Conclusion: Correctness and consistency describe different properties: repeated agreement can be consistently wrong, and a correct majority can contain substantial disagreement.

Cohen’s kappa. agreement between two labelers or a labeler and a reference after subtracting the agreement expected from their label frequencies.
\[
κ = \frac{p_o-p_e}{1-p_e}
\tag{4.4}\]
Here \(p_o\) is the observed fraction of matching labels. The marginal label shares determine \(p_e\): for each label, multiply the two labelers’ shares and sum those products. Kappa scales the agreement above this expectation by the remaining possible agreement. When \(p_e=1\), its denominator is zero and kappa is undefined; label prevalence and the confusion counts remain necessary context.

Worked calculation: chance-adjusted agreement on 20 cases
Observed agreement: TP = 7 and TN = 9, so \(p_o = 16/20 = 0.80\).
Label shares: The reference is 50% positive; the judge is 40% positive and 60% negative.
Expected agreement: \(p_e = 0.50 \times 0.40 + 0.50 \times 0.60 = 0.50\).
Kappa: κ = (0.80 − 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.50) = 0.60.
Conclusion: The evaluator agrees on 80% of cases, and 60% of the possible agreement beyond the marginal expectation is realized.







Figure 4.9: Repeated judgments expose rows whose verdict changes even when the input does not.



The evaluator configuration records the judge temperature and model revision. Temperature zero still allows variation across providers, kernels, or model updates. Raw responses and parse failures remain part of the evidence; malformed JSON is an evaluator failure rather than a discarded vote.

section: 4.8 Structuring evaluation prompts as decision trees
text:
4.8 Structuring evaluation prompts as decision trees
Repeated verdicts reveal unstable cases but not the structural reason a prompt is unstable. A natural-language evaluator can contain contradictory overrides, missing tie-breaks, and ambiguous scope. A decision tree makes the flow, rule precedence, and ambiguous cases inspectable while keeping every node linked to source text.






Figure 4.10: A prompt can be inspected as ordered decisions, overrides, and terminal verdicts.



The implementation uses three model calls. TREE_SYS extracts entry, decision, subtask, rule, verdict, and side-note nodes. ORDER_SYS moves short-circuit overrides before the decisions they control and leaves the default fallback last. ISSUE_SYS reports gray zones, contradictions, redundancy, missing tie-breaks, and ambiguous scope.

Code example: Three-stage prompt analysis with inspectable intermediate representations.

# Abbreviated: each helper returns structured, source-anchored output.
def analyze(prompt_text):
    draft = extract_tree(prompt_text)
    tree = reorder_tree(prompt_text, draft)
    issues = find_issues(prompt_text, tree)
    return {
        "prompt_text": prompt_text,
        "draft": draft,
        "tree": tree,
        "issues": issues,
    }

Code walkthrough
Extraction: extract_tree converts natural-language instructions into candidate decision and verdict nodes anchored to prompt text.
Precedence: reorder_tree places short-circuit and override rules before the decisions they control.
Audit: find_issues identifies gray zones, contradictions, redundancy, missing tie-breaks, and ambiguous scope.
Returned evidence: The original prompt, extracted draft, reordered tree, and issue list remain together so the reviewer can compare each transformation with source wording.
Result: Separating extraction, ordering, and critique makes changes inspectable. It does not guarantee that a model preserved every rule; quoted source anchors and branch coverage still need checking.
Limits: Every node retains a verbatim source anchor. Mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive branches reduce ambiguity, and human review remains part of release-gate approval.


Before-and-after decision flow
Before: Mark unsupported answers as bad unless they are harmless, except when the context strongly implies them. The terms harmless and strongly implies have no ordered test, so the same claim can reach different verdicts.
Proposed policy after review: missing context → needs_review; otherwise, any claim contradicted by the context → unsupported; otherwise, any factual claim without supporting evidence → unsupported; otherwise → supported.
This proposal removes the undefined harmlessness exception and adds a review outcome. Those are policy changes, not mere reordering, and require approval. If adopted, the evaluator schema and aggregation must also support needs_review; the earlier binary loop would reject it. Until those changes are approved, the original ambiguity remains recorded as unresolved.
The comparison measures disagreement and adjudication time on the same ambiguous-case slice, and checks which original rules were retained, clarified, or deliberately changed.







Figure 4.11: Long-context evaluation becomes tractable when claims are decomposed and checked locally.



Long answers make one global groundedness decision too complex. A stronger design decomposes the output into atomic claims, retrieves or selects the relevant context for each claim, scores the claims independently, and aggregates with an explicit policy. The aggregation rule states whether one unsupported critical claim fails the whole answer or produces a fractional score.

4.9 Evaluating agent trajectories and tool use
A decision tree makes one evaluator’s logic explicit. An agent can still reach a plausible final answer through unsafe, wasteful, or accidental intermediate actions. Trajectory evidence, tool definitions, recovery behavior, and the terminal output together describe agent quality.






Figure 4.12: Agent evaluation includes the trajectory as well as the final answer.



Agent evaluation needs at least three scopes. Outcome metrics test whether the task was completed. Trajectory metrics inspect tool choice, order, arguments, repeated actions, and policy violations. Runtime metrics record latency, token use, tool cost, retries, and failure recovery. A final-answer judge alone cannot tell whether the system leaked data, relied on a tool error, or succeeded by chance.

Scope
Example metric
Evidence




Outcome

Final artifact and deterministic verifier


Trajectory

Ordered tool-call spans and state changes


Retrieval

Robustness

Efficiency
Cost, latency, calls, tokens, steps
Trace-level resource measurements







Worked calculation: a plausible answer reached through an invalid action
Outcome: The agent returns the correct invoice total, so the final-answer score is 1.0.
Trajectory: It first calls an unapproved broad customer-search tool. It then calls the approved invoice tool, which times out, and retries that invoice call successfully.
Robustness: The timeout recovery succeeds, but the first call violates the tool allowlist and exposes more data than the task requires.
Efficiency: Three calls, including one retry, cost more and take longer than the reference one-call path.
Decision: The case fails the policy gate despite a correct terminal answer; the trace supplies the invalid action and its arguments for diagnosis.
Conclusion: Outcome, trajectory, robustness, and efficiency scores reveal different properties of the same run.

4.10 Turning production failures into evaluation cases
Telemetry, drift signals, experiments, evaluators, and trajectory evidence are now versioned. They create value only when production failures become reproducible cases and validated changes return safely. The loop contains evidence capture, triage, dataset expansion, experimentation, release, and post-release verification.






Figure 4.13: Production evidence becomes research cases, then validated changes return to production.



The loop uses an ordered evidence path:

Captured evidence. Low-quality outputs, failed traces, drift alerts, user feedback, and incidents are sampled under a controlled retention policy.
Triage. Each case receives a failure category and a responsible component: data, prompt, model, retrieval, tool, runtime, or product policy.
Replay case. The relevant context, expected behavior, and evaluator definition form a minimized reproducible case.
Suite expansion. The case enters a versioned evaluation suite together with nearby cases that reveal broader failure patterns.
Controlled experiment. One identified component changes, and the recorded run compares quality, latency, cost, and safety slices.
Candidate release. The validated change becomes a new serving bundle that passes the performance and quality checks from Chapter 3.
Post-release verification. The same production signal and guardrail metrics remain under observation while rollback stays available through the evidence window.


Incident-to-regression-case example
A support answer cites an expired policy after retrieval selected an older document version. The minimized replay case retains the query, retrieved IDs, timestamps, answer, expected current-policy citation, bundle IDs, and evaluator verdict.
The candidate change adds an effective-date filter. The expanded suite includes the original case, nearby policy dates, and a control set of undated documents. Release evidence compares retrieval recall, groundedness, latency, and authorization behavior before promotion.


Chapter 4 summary
Core mechanisms: OpenTelemetry standardized spans and traces; distribution drift detection; repeatable LLM-as-a-judge groundedness evaluation; decision tree prompt structuring.
Governing tradeoffs: Evaluator prompt expressiveness vs. deterministic reproducibility; full-corpus sampling cost vs. statistical significance.
Failure modes & defenses: Cohen’s kappa chance-adjusted agreement; regression gates that preserve production failure cases.


Chapter 4 mastery check
Can one request be joined across gateway, router, engine, retriever, evaluator, and release identities?
Can a drift alert be separated from confirmed quality loss and connected to delayed ground truth?
Can an experiment be reproduced from immutable cases, prompt, model, runtime, evaluator, and raw verdicts?
Can evaluator correctness, consistency, latency, and cost be measured before the evaluator becomes a release gate?
Can a production failure become a replay case whose post-release signal is verified?


Carry-forward result
The evidence layer now correlates telemetry, drift, AI traces, experiments, calibrated evaluators, and replayable failure cases. Chapter 5 places the durable and derived data they consume.

text:
5.1 Matching storage to AI access patterns
Which storage system fits each artifact, and how does retrieval state remain correct as data and embeddings change? Chapter 4 produced traces, datasets, checkpoints, evaluation cases, and experiment records that outlive individual processes. Access patterns lead to storage semantics and then to a versioned vector-retrieval system with reproducible derived indexes.
The three panels connect durable storage to embedding and index state, then to the retrieval path that balances relevance, latency, and reproducibility.
Checkpoints, training samples, request logs, and retrieval indexes need different storage behavior. Some need partial file updates, others shared paths, immutable object identities, or low-latency local reads. Object size, concurrency, durability, and access pattern determine the suitable storage category.
POSIX-style interfaces expose file operations such as opening a path, reading bytes at an offset, and renaming a file. An object interface instead reads or replaces a value identified by a key, often through an S3-compatible API. NVMe is a storage interface commonly used by fast local solid-state drives. These names describe different layers: an interface, an object API, and a device access technology are not interchangeable storage guarantees.
Access pattern. the combination of object size, operation mix, concurrency, locality, sharing, durability, consistency, latency, throughput, and lifecycle requirements for a dataset or artifact.
The hierarchy is a movement plan, not a ranking. GPU memory and local NVMe are fast and scarce. Shared file systems support concurrent workers. Object storage provides durable, scalable namespaces but does not behave like a local file system. Archive tiers trade retrieval delay for lower cost. The correct design stages data between tiers without confusing a cache with the source of truth.

section: 5.3 Preventing GPU idle time during data loading
text:
5.3 Preventing GPU idle time during data loading
Storage semantics now match the artifact type. A training job can still leave GPUs idle if decoding, metadata, network reads, or sample assembly cannot fill device queues. The input path is a pipeline of buffers, workers, shards, and observable backpressure.






Figure 5.4: Each pipeline stage uses storage according to durability, sharing, and latency needs.



The path usually includes durable source objects, a conversion or sharding stage, shared or local cache, CPU workers, pinned host memory, host-to-device transfer, and the accelerator. The slowest sustained stage bounds throughput. Prefetching hides latency only while downstream consumption does not outrun the buffer.
Pinned host memory cannot be paged out while a transfer uses it, allowing the accelerator to copy from a stable host buffer. Backpressure occurs when a downstream queue fills and slows the workers supplying it. For example, fast storage does not prevent GPU idle time when CPU decompression cannot prepare the next batch; increasing the read queue then consumes memory without raising training throughput.

Sequential-read shards. Moderately large immutable shards reduce metadata operations and produce longer reads.
Deterministic partitioning. Each data-parallel rank receives a reproducible sample stream whose seed, epoch, padding, and sharding policy are recorded.
Parallel decoding. Worker processes overlap parsing and augmentation within CPU, memory, and open-file limits.
Identity-based caching. Immutable dataset or shard identities connect cache hit rate, capacity, and eviction behavior to a specific input version.
Queue measurements. Batch-fetch time, GPU idle gaps, bytes/s, IOPS, cache hit rate, and failed reads reveal backpressure.

This abbreviated loop assumes a map-style dataset, an initialized distributed process group, the same seed on every rank, and workers > 0. move_to_device recursively transfers the batch tensors; train_step performs the training update described in Chapter 2.

Code example: Deterministic distributed data loading with prefetched host-to-device transfer.


loader = DataLoader(
    dataset,
    batch_size=batch_size,
    sampler=DistributedSampler(dataset, shuffle=True, seed=seed),
    num_workers=workers,
    pin_memory=True,
    persistent_workers=True,
    prefetch_factor=2,
)

for epoch in range(start_epoch, epochs):
    loader.sampler.set_epoch(epoch)
    for batch in loader:
        batch = move_to_device(batch, non_blocking=True)
        loss = train_step(batch)

Code walkthrough
Rank partition: DistributedSampler shuffles indices reproducibly and divides them among ranks. Its default padding repeats some indices when the dataset size is not divisible by the number of ranks, keeping rank step counts equal.
Epoch state: set_epoch changes the reproducible shuffle order between epochs.
Host pipeline: Worker processes, persistence, and prefetching prepare future batches while the accelerator executes the current batch.
Transfer path: Pinned host memory and non_blocking=True permit asynchronous transfer when tensor layout and CUDA stream usage support overlap.
Result: Correct partitioning protects statistical semantics, while buffering and transfer overlap protect accelerator utilization.
Limits: More workers or prefetch slots can exhaust CPU, host memory, file descriptors, or storage bandwidth. Fetch time and queue depth reveal the limit; larger values are not automatically better.

For five samples and two ranks, an unshuffled default sampler extends [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] to [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0]. Rank 0 reads [0, 2, 4] and rank 1 reads [1, 3, 0]: index 0 repeats. Setting the sampler’s drop_last=True instead drops the tail so each rank receives two samples. The choice changes which examples contribute to an epoch; it is especially important when counting evaluation cases, where padded duplicates can bias a metric.
GPUDirect Storage (GDS) provides a different transfer path: compatible storage software transfers bytes directly to GPU memory without an intermediate CPU-memory bounce buffer. This can reduce host-memory traffic and CPU transfer overhead when GPU-side processing consumes the data. The CPU still sets up the operation. GDS requires a supported storage/filesystem and transfer configuration; a fallback may still use host memory. It does not remove CPU decoding that the application still performs, and pin_memory=True alone does not enable it. A useful comparison measures end-to-end batch readiness, not only storage-to-GPU copy bandwidth.

section: 5.4 Writing recoverable checkpoints atomically
text:
5.4 Writing recoverable checkpoints atomically
Chapter 2 defined checkpoint contents and recovery objectives. The remaining piece is a storage protocol that keeps a partial multi-rank save hidden. Fast landing, completeness validation, atomic publication, and copying across failure domains form that protocol.






Figure 5.5: A fast checkpoint lands locally, copies asynchronously to shared storage, and archives to object storage.



A distributed checkpoint is a set of shards plus metadata, not merely a directory. Each writer first saves to a temporary generation. A coordinator verifies the expected world size, file hashes, byte counts, and training-state metadata. Only then does it publish a small completion manifest or pointer. Restore clients ignore generations without that commit marker.
For a file-system implementation, generation g42 first contains all completed shards. Writers finish the required flush/durability operations, and the coordinator writes a temporary manifest containing their identities and checksums. A same-filesystem atomic rename publishes that manifest; directory durability also depends on the filesystem’s persistence protocol. A crash before publication leaves an ignored incomplete generation, while a crash afterward leaves a complete manifest pointing to durable shards. An object-store implementation uses completed immutable shard objects followed by a final manifest PUT, relying on the store’s documented visibility and durability behavior rather than a directory rename.
A completed local generation is not yet protected against loss of that node. The durable recovery point advances only when the required copy in the other failure domain is complete and verified. While an asynchronous copy is pending, recovery from node loss may still use the preceding durable generation.



Table 5.3: A checkpoint becomes trustworthy only after completeness, durability, and restore evidence exist.










Phase
Storage role
Required evidence




Fast landing
Local NVMe or high-throughput shared scratch
Writer rank, shard name, size, checksum


Committed generation
Shared namespace visible to all workers
Complete shard set and atomic manifest


Replicate
Object storage in another failure domain
Copy status and verified object hashes


Retention
Durable object or archive tier
Policy, expiry, legal/security constraints


Restore test
Fresh allocation and staging cache
Measured recovery time and resumed state identity







Worked calculation: checkpoint interval versus failure loss
Given: A job produces 18 minutes of useful work between checkpoints and needs 2 minutes to write each checkpoint.
Failure position: In a simplified model where failure is uniformly distributed within the 18-minute useful-work interval, expected lost useful work is half that interval: 9 minutes. Failure during a checkpoint write needs separate accounting because the new generation may not yet be committed.
Recovery work: A node replacement and restore take 6 minutes.
Expected interruption: The 9 minutes of expected lost work plus 6 minutes for replacement and restore produce about 15 minutes of interruption, excluding recurring checkpoint overhead.
Decision: A shorter interval is justified only when reduced expected loss exceeds the added write load and pause.
Conclusion: Checkpoint policy trades recurring overhead against expected lost work; restore testing supplies the evidence.

text:
5.5 Measuring storage performance for AI workloads
The correct storage category and protocol are now selected. Performance claims still fail when a benchmark uses a different block size, operation mix, cache state, or client count than the ML workload. A representative benchmark relates I/O operations to transferred bytes and includes the intended concurrency and tail behavior.






Figure 5.6: At the same 25,000 operations/s, 4 KiB transfers produce about 97.7 MiB/s, while 1 MiB transfers would require 25,000 MiB/s; in practice, larger transfers can hit a byte-rate ceiling and reduce achievable IOPS.



\[
B = \mathrm{IOPS} \cdot S_{\mathrm{block}}
\tag{5.1}\]
Here \(B\) is transferred bytes per second, IOPS is completed input/output operations per second, and \(S_{\mathrm{block}}\) is bytes transferred per operation. For mixed transfer sizes, it is the mean size over completed operations in the same measurement window. Multiplying the operation count by the bytes per operation gives the transferred bytes.

Worked calculation: the same IOPS with two transfer sizes
Operation rate: The storage path completes 25,000 read operations per second.
Small transfers: At 4 KiB per operation, throughput is 102,400,000 bytes/s, about 97.7 MiB/s.
Large transfers: At 1 MiB per operation, the same operation rate would imply 25,000 MiB/s if the system and network could sustain it.
Constraint: In practice, achievable IOPS falls as transfer size grows and bandwidth limits become active.
Conclusion: IOPS is meaningful only with transfer size, concurrency, latency, cache state, and operation mix.

The equality is descriptive, not a promise that either term remains constant. Increasing block size may reduce achievable IOPS; increasing clients may expose network, metadata, or server limits. A complete result includes read/write mix, direct-versus-cached mode, queue depth, client count, object or file size distribution, warm-up, duration, percentiles, and failure rate.
Synthetic storage tests can omit application parsing, metadata work, temporary burst credits, and competing clients. Comparing them with an actual data-loader or checkpoint trace shows whether the measured storage rate translates into less GPU idle time or a shorter recoverable save.

section: 5.6 Migrating safely between embedding versions
text:
5.6 Migrating safely between embedding versions
Durable source records and efficient movement are established. Semantic retrieval needs a derived numerical representation whose model, preprocessing, and distance convention remain consistent. Embeddings, chunk identities, metadata, and score direction define the index inputs.
An embedding migration preserves those identities in a new collection. Backfill, validation, and the traffic switch then put the new collection into service, as described in Section 5.9.
Embedding. a fixed-length numeric vector produced by a specified model and preprocessing pipeline to represent an item for comparison.






Figure 5.7: Embeddings place heterogeneous items into one numerical vector space.



The vector is derived state. Its identity includes the source object and version, chunk start and end offsets, normalization, embedding model and revision, dimensionality, language or modality, and transformation code. The original text or media remains the durable evidence; embeddings and indexes remain rebuildable from it.
\[
\cos\left(q,x\right) = \frac{q^{T}x}{\left\lVert q\right\rVert \cdot \left\lVert x\right\rVert}
\tag{5.2}\]
The query vector \(q\) and candidate vector \(x\) have the same dimension and nonzero length. The transpose in \(q^T x\) forms their dot product, and \(\lVert q\rVert\) and \(\lVert x\rVert\) are Euclidean lengths. Dividing by both lengths leaves the angle-dependent score. For real vectors, cosine similarity lies between −1 and 1; larger values mean more aligned directions. A zero vector has no defined direction.

Worked calculation: cosine similarity of two vectors
Vectors: The query is (1, 2) and the candidate is (2, 1).
Dot product: The aligned component products are 2 and 2, so their sum is 4.
Norms: Each vector has Euclidean norm √5, so the norm product is 5.
Similarity: Dividing 4 by 5 gives cosine similarity 0.8.
Conclusion: The vectors point in a similar but not identical direction; multiplying either vector by a positive scalar would not change the cosine score.


Code example: Reference cosine-similarity implementation with dimensionality and zero-vector checks.

import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(query: np.ndarray, candidate: np.ndarray) -> float:
    if query.ndim != 1 or candidate.ndim != 1 or query.shape != candidate.shape:
        raise ValueError("vectors must be one-dimensional with equal shapes")
    if not np.isfinite(query).all() or not np.isfinite(candidate).all():
        raise ValueError("vectors must contain finite values")
    denominator = np.linalg.norm(query) * np.linalg.norm(candidate)
    if denominator == 0:
        raise ValueError("cosine similarity is undefined for a zero vector")
    return float(np.dot(query, candidate) / denominator)

Code walkthrough
Schema check: The function accepts finite one-dimensional arrays of equal shape before computing a score.
Domain check: A zero norm is rejected because the cosine denominator would be zero and direction is undefined.
Numerator: np.dot measures aligned component magnitude.
Normalization: Dividing by both Euclidean norms removes vector magnitude and returns a scalar direction score.
Result: The function implements cosine similarity and makes two otherwise silent input-validation failures explicit.
Limits: Production retrieval usually uses a vectorized library or index, so dtype, normalization, numerical tolerance, and similarity-versus-distance direction are part of the implementation.







Figure 5.8: Dot product, cosine similarity, and cosine distance use different score directions and ranges.




Score definition
Thresholds require recalibration when the embedding model, normalization, or distance metric changes.
The score definition states whether larger or smaller is better, its valid range, and every transformation applied before ranking.

section: 5.7 Choosing a vector index for approximate search
text:
5.7 Choosing a vector index for approximate search
Every candidate can be scored exactly when the collection is small. At production scale, exhaustive comparison makes query cost grow with the entire corpus. Approximate nearest-neighbor structures prune candidates, and their accuracy-latency trade-off is measured against an exact reference.
Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search. retrieval that uses an index to find likely close vectors without comparing the query with every vector.






Figure 5.9: An Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index narrows candidates before exact or approximate distance computation.



The comparison separates an exact reference method from graph, partition, and compression-based approximations.



Table 5.4: ANN families make different compromises among recall, latency, build cost, update behavior, and memory.











Method
Core idea
Strength
Trade-off




Flat / exact
Scoring every vector
Reference-quality results and simple updates
Latency and compute grow with corpus size


HNSW
Navigating a layered proximity graph
Strong recall and low query latency
Memory-heavy graph; build/update tuning matters


IVF
Probing selected coarse clusters
Controls scanned fraction with nprobe
Misses neighbors in unprobed cells


Product quantization
Compact codebooks for vector subspaces
Large memory reduction and fast approximate distance
Compression reduces score fidelity


IVF-PQ
Probing coarse cells and scoring compressed codes
Scales large collections within memory limits
Two approximation stages require calibration






Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) links nearby vectors in a graph with progressively sparser upper layers. A query first moves through these upper layers to find a useful entry region, then explores more candidates in the dense base layer. Graph links avoid scanning every stored vector, but a limited search can miss the true nearest neighbor.
An inverted-file (IVF) index assigns vectors to coarse clusters during construction. At query time it compares the query with cluster representatives and scans only the selected lists. For eight clusters and nprobe=2, six lists remain unsearched. Increasing the probe count exposes more vectors and costs more distance calculations; a close vector just across an unprobed cluster boundary explains a recall miss.
Product quantization (PQ) splits each vector into subvectors and stores the nearest codebook entry ID for each part. For example, (1, 2, 8, 9) can be split into (1, 2) and (8, 9), approximated by entries (1, 1) and (8, 10). Two 8-bit IDs occupy two bytes rather than sixteen bytes for four FP32 values, excluding the shared codebooks. Lookup tables combine query-to-entry distances; the approximation can change close rankings. IVF-PQ first selects coarse lists and then scores compressed vectors, often encoding each vector’s difference from its cluster representative. It therefore has both missed-list and compressed-distance errors.






Figure 5.10: IVF-PQ combines coarse partitioning with compressed residual codes.



HNSW’s efSearch and IVF’s probe count control query search effort. Graph connectivity and quantization code size are construction choices that affect the resulting index and usually require rebuilding to change. Higher query effort usually improves recall and consumes more latency or compute. Index build time, memory amplification, background compaction, and update lag belong in capacity planning.

An HNSW query trace
Entry: Starting from the graph’s stored entry point, the query greedily follows closer neighbors in the upper layers and descends to the base layer.
Expansion: Base-layer search keeps a queue of unexplored candidates and a retained nearest-candidate set whose width is controlled by efSearch. This is not a hard cap on visited nodes or distance calculations.
Termination: Search stops when the closest queued candidate cannot improve the retained set under the algorithm’s stopping rule. The best k retained identities are returned; an unexplored region can still contain a true nearer neighbor.
Trade-off: Increasing efSearch expands more candidates and generally raises recall while increasing tail latency and CPU work; the chosen value is measured on the target corpus and filter mix.
Conclusion: The trace makes HNSW’s quality–latency control visible instead of treating efSearch as a universal constant.

section: 5.8 Combining dense and sparse retrieval
text:
5.8 Combining dense and sparse retrieval
ANN search retrieves semantically close vectors. Dense similarity can miss exact identifiers, rare names, or domain-specific lexical matches. Access-control and date constraints are separate rules that ranking scores cannot enforce. A staged retriever gives each component a specific candidate, filtering, scoring, or packing role.






Figure 5.11: Hybrid retrieval merges dense and sparse candidates before cross-encoder reranking.




Early filtering. Tenant, access-control, language, date, document-type, and lifecycle constraints narrow the search as early as the index permits.
Dense candidates. The embedding index returns candidates under the metric and model revision paired with the stored vectors.
Sparse candidates. Lexical retrieval adds exact tokens, identifiers, and rare terms.
Rank fusion. A stated normalization or rank-fusion rule combines the ranked lists without relying on incomparable raw scores.
Reranking. A more expensive cross-encoder or domain scorer evaluates the reduced candidate set.
Context assembly. Deduplication, ordering, token-budget fitting, and retained source IDs produce the final evidence context.

BM25 is a lexical ranking method: matching query terms contribute more when they are uncommon in the collection, repeated occurrences have diminishing additional value, and document-length normalization reduces the advantage of long documents. An exact error code such as ERR-1842 can therefore retrieve a precise troubleshooting paragraph that a dense model ranks poorly. A cross-encoder then reads the query and each candidate together to produce a relevance score. That joint computation captures interactions a separately stored vector may miss, but repeats model work for every candidate.
Pre-filtering restricts eligible records before nearest-neighbor selection; post-filtering removes ineligible results afterward. If a top-10 search returns only two documents the caller may access, post-filtering leaves two results even when many eligible documents exist elsewhere. Overfetching or filter-aware search can improve coverage, with additional work. Permission checks still occur before unauthorized text reaches a reranker or prompt, regardless of the index’s filtering implementation.
\[
\operatorname{RRF}\left(d\right) = \sum_{r \in \left\{\mathrm{dense},\mathrm{sparse}\right\}} \frac{1}{k+\operatorname{rank}_r\left(d\right)}
\tag{5.3}\]
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) adds rank-based contributions for document \(d\) from each list \(r\). Ranks start at 1; a document absent from a list contributes zero. The positive smoothing constant \(k\) reduces the dominance of the very first ranks and is distinct from the number of results requested in top-k search. Raw dense and lexical scores never need to share a numeric scale.
With smoothing constant 60, document A at dense rank 1 and sparse rank 3 scores \(1/61+1/63\approx0.03227\). Document B at dense rank 2 and sparse rank 1 scores \(1/62+1/61\approx0.03252\), so B ranks first after fusion. The candidate-window sizes matter: a document omitted by both first-stage retrievers cannot be recovered by fusion.
The following abbreviated pipeline assumes that both indexes enforce acl_filter before returning text and that fusion deduplicates records by stable document/chunk identity. Each helper returns candidates with their source IDs intact.

Code example: Hybrid retrieval pipeline with versioned embedding, authorization, fusion, reranking, and citation packing.


query_vector = embed(query, model=EMBEDDING_VERSION)

dense  = vector_index.search(query_vector, top_k=80, filters=acl_filter)
sparse = lexical_index.search(query, top_k=80, filters=acl_filter)
fused  = reciprocal_rank_fusion(dense, sparse)
ranked = cross_encoder.rerank(query, fused[:40])

context = pack_with_citations(ranked[:8], token_budget=6000)

Code walkthrough
Vector-space identity: EMBEDDING_VERSION selects the same model and preprocessing identity used to build the collection.
Access control: acl_filter constrains both candidate generators before unauthorized content can enter fusion or the prompt.
Candidate fusion: Dense and sparse lists are merged by rank rather than by adding raw scores with incompatible scales.
Cost funnel: The cross-encoder scores only 40 fused candidates, and the packer retains eight cited items inside the token budget.
Result: Each stage narrows or validates state while preserving source identities for the generated answer and later evaluation.
Limits: The sketch omits timeouts, deduplication policy, score calibration, empty-result behavior, freshness checks, and trace emission; those belong to the production requirements.

5.9 Running vector databases as stateful services
The retrieval algorithm is now explicit. A production vector system also ingests updates, persists state, replicates data, rebuilds indexes, backs up metadata, and survives version changes. Durable source records and derived collections have separate lifecycle and recovery rules.






Figure 5.12: Build and query paths meet at a rebuildable Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index backed by source-of-truth storage.



The build path reads versioned source records, applies deterministic chunking and embedding, writes vector records with metadata, and constructs an index. The query path embeds one query, applies authorization and filters, retrieves candidates, reranks, and returns source identifiers. Both paths share the same schema and embedding version.






Figure 5.13: A vector database is a stateful service with ingestion, serving, persistence, replication, and backups.



The recovery map distinguishes authoritative records from derived vector state that may be restored or rebuilt.



Table 5.5: Vector recovery depends on knowing which state is authoritative and which state is reproducible.










State
System of record
Recovery action




Original document/media
Durable object or document store
Exact-version read by immutable ID

Recreate chunk text and ordering


Embedding record

Restore compatible snapshot or rebuild

Authoritative application/identity store
Reapply and verify before serving


Query/evaluation traces
Governed telemetry store
Replay workload-matched cases after recovery












Figure 5.14: Embedding versions require controlled upserts, reindexing, rollback, and full re-embedding.



An embedding-model change creates a new vector space. Mixing old and new vectors in one index usually makes scores meaningless. A versioned collection receives the backfill, count and quality checks, shadow or canary queries, and then an alias switch; the previous collection remains available for rollback. Tombstones or source-version reconciliation keep deleted content out of retrieval.
An alias is a stable application-facing name pointing to a particular collection. The switch must update the query-embedding configuration together with that collection choice; new query vectors against old document vectors would break the pairing even if both have the same dimension.

Freeze the source. Record the source snapshot, chunking revision, access-control metadata, and deletion watermark that define the migration input.
Build beside production. Write embeddings and the ANN index into a new versioned collection; leave the current alias untouched while workers retry.
Reconcile. Compare expected and actual source, chunk, vector, tenant, dimension, and delete counts; sample retrieval cases against the prior collection.
Switch and retain. Promote the alias only after the gates pass, keep the previous collection for rollback, and record the immutable alias transition in the manifest.

If ingestion continues during backfill, the source snapshot also records a change-log position. Suppose document D is updated after the snapshot and E is deleted. The backfill initially writes the old D and E; a catch-up pass then applies the new D version and E’s tombstone before the switch. A short ingestion pause or an agreed cutover watermark closes the final gap while counts and versions are checked. Rollback also reconciles later deletions and permission changes; retaining an old collection does not authorize serving content whose access was revoked.

section: 5.10 Balancing retrieval quality and latency
text:
5.10 Balancing retrieval quality and latency
The vector service has a defined build path, query path, and migration method. Index microbenchmarks alone cannot show whether the right evidence reaches the LLM under production filters and load. Retrieval quality, tail latency, resource use, freshness, and end-to-end grounded-answer quality are measured on intended workload slices.
\[
\mathrm{Recall}@k = \frac{\lvert R_k \cap G \rvert}{\lvert G \rvert}
\tag{5.4}\]
Here \(R_k\) is the set of retrieved top-k document identities, \(G\) is the reference set judged relevant, \(\cap\) selects shared identities, and vertical bars count set members. Queries with no known relevant documents have a zero denominator and need a separate stated reporting policy. This task-relevance measure differs from ANN recall, which compares an approximate index’s neighbors with an exact-search top-k reference. An index can closely reproduce exact neighbors while the embedding itself retrieves poor task evidence.

Worked calculation: recall at five for one query
Reference set: Human labels identify four relevant documents.
Retrieved set: The top five results contain three of those four relevant documents plus two irrelevant documents.
Intersection: Three retrieved identities belong to the reference-relevant set.
Recall: Dividing 3 by 4 gives recall@5 of 0.75.
Conclusion: The score measures evidence coverage, not ranking quality or whether the generator cites and uses the evidence correctly.

Precision@k instead divides relevant retrieved documents by the number returned at the stated cutoff. Mean reciprocal rank (MRR) measures how soon the first relevant result appears: each query contributes \(1/r\) for its first relevant rank \(r\), or zero when none appears within the measured list, and the mean is taken over queries.
Normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) also distinguishes degrees of relevance. One common convention gives rank \(j\) a gain \((2^{g_j}-1)/\log_2(j+1)\), where \(g_j\) is its nonnegative relevance grade. Summing gives DCG; dividing by the DCG of the ideal grade ordering at the same cutoff gives nDCG. The gain convention, cutoff, and treatment of queries with no positive grades must be recorded.
For a three-document ranking with grades [0, 3, 1], both positively graded documents appear: precision@3 is \(2/3\), recall@3 is 1 if those are the only relevant documents, and reciprocal rank is \(1/2\). Using exponential gain, DCG is \(0+7/\log_2 3+1/2\approx4.917\). The ideal order [3, 1, 0] has DCG \(7+1/\log_2 3\approx7.631\), giving nDCG@3 about 0.644. Recall does not change when the irrelevant first result moves to the end, but the ranking metrics improve.






Figure 5.15: Recall, latency, and memory pull vector search in different directions.









Figure 5.16: Honest vector-system benchmarks measure recall and tail latency on the intended workload.



A reproducible acceptance criterion includes retrieval quality, latency, resources, freshness, reliability, and end-to-end answer quality.

Dimension
Minimum measurement
Required slice




Retrieval quality

Query type, language, tenant, document age


Latency
p50/p95/p99 build and query stage timing
Concurrency, corpus size, filter selectivity


Resources
Memory, CPU/GPU, storage, network, index size
Steady state and rebuild


Freshness

Reliability

Worked calculation: choosing a retrieval operating point
Candidate A: Recall@5 is 0.82 at p99 query latency of 95 ms with a 1.4 GB index.
Candidate B: Recall@5 is 0.79 at p99 latency of 42 ms with a 0.8 GB index.
Candidate C: Recall@5 is 0.86 at p99 latency of 180 ms with a 2.1 GB index.
Decision: If the product requires recall \(\geq\) 0.80 and p99 \(\leq\) 120 ms, Candidate A is feasible; B misses recall and C misses latency. The same comparison is repeated on tenant and document-age slices before release.
Conclusion: A Pareto comparison makes the selected operating point explicit and keeps a single aggregate score from hiding a failed constraint.

Core mechanisms: Tiered storage architectures (POSIX, S3, NVMe); GPUDirect Storage data loading; HNSW proximity graph vector indexing; hybrid sparse-dense reciprocal rank fusion.
Governing tradeoffs: Vector index recall vs. p99 search latency; build time and RAM footprint vs. search throughput; dense semantic matching vs. exact keyword precision.
Failure modes & defenses: Atomic checkpoint commits preventing partial writes; versioned embedding index migrations preventing representation mismatch.

6.1 From manual scripts to automated pipelines
How can the system reproduce a multi-step ML result after partial failure, schedule delay, code change, or operator handoff? Chapter 5 established durable artifacts and rebuildable derived state. Dependency graphs replace manual command sequences with tasks that have explicit inputs, outputs, resources, retries, and evidence.

The task implementation performs domain work such as preprocessing or training. The artifact store carries large outputs. The metadata store carries orchestration state and small references.

section: 6.2 Scheduling task dependencies with directed acyclic graphs
text:
6.2 Scheduling task dependencies with directed acyclic graphs
The workflow’s responsibilities are separated. The orchestrator still needs an unambiguous rule for which tasks may run and which work can happen in parallel. Tasks are nodes, and prerequisite relationships are directed edges without cycles.
Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). a graph whose directed edges encode dependency order and whose lack of cycles guarantees that a topological execution order exists.






Figure 6.2: A DAG makes dependencies and parallel branches explicit.



An edge A → B means B cannot start successfully until A’s required output is available; A does not directly invoke B. Independent branches can execute concurrently. A cycle leaves every node in the loop waiting, so feedback over time is represented by separate DAG runs or external events.
\[
T_{\mathrm{DAG}} \ge \max_{p \in P} \sum_{i \in p} t_i
\tag{6.1}\]
Here, \(T_{\mathrm{DAG}}\) is the observed duration of one DAG run. \(P\) is the set of start-to-finish dependency paths, \(p\) is one such path, and \(t_i\) is the duration of task \(i\) on that path. The longest path sets a lower bound because queueing, resource shortages, and retries can make the real run take longer.

Worked calculation: critical path in a two-branch pipeline
Shared start: Validation takes 4 minutes.
Training branch: Training takes 38 minutes and model evaluation takes 8 minutes.
Retrieval branch: Embedding takes 20 minutes and index validation takes 6 minutes.
Shared release: The promotion gate takes 3 minutes after both branches finish.
Path sums: Adding the task durations gives 53 minutes for the training path and 33 minutes for the retrieval path.
Conclusion: The 53-minute training path controls the lower bound; accelerating the 33-minute branch alone cannot reduce end-to-end time below 53 minutes.


Critical-path implication
Doubling workers does not accelerate a strictly serial chain. Only changes to tasks on the critical path reduce the completion-time lower bound.
A slow off-path task can still consume capacity and delay later runs, so capacity and critical-path analysis remain separate.

6.3 Defining immutable task inputs and outputs
The DAG states dependency order. A task called ‘train’ is still too vague to retry safely or reproduce after an image, dataset, or configuration changes. Every task has immutable inputs, explicit outputs, resource needs, failure behavior, and validation.
Task specification. the complete contract for one pipeline task: identity, immutable inputs, outputs, runtime, resources, retry behavior, validation, and side effects.
Idempotent task. a task whose repeated execution with the same declared inputs reaches the same externally visible result without corrupting state or duplicating effects.
Specific task fields make repeatability inspectable by both the scheduler and the next task.

Freezes libraries and system dependencies

section: 6.5 Running complete ML workflows in Airflow
text:
6.5 Running complete ML workflows in Airflow
The control-plane roles and task description are explicit. The abbreviated Python definition describes dependencies without performing expensive work during import. DATASET_MANIFEST, EMBEDDING_VERSION, EVAL_SUITE, and COLLECTION_ID are immutable identities resolved before the run starts. Lightweight DAG parsing leaves domain code to isolated task runtimes.
The abbreviated pipeline.embed application accepts COLLECTION_ID through its --collection argument, writes that collection, and publishes its completion manifest outside Airflow’s metadata database. The evaluation task reads the same collection identity after the dependency succeeds. The fixed name therefore represents an agreed input/output location, not a large task result passed through Airflow.

Code example: Airflow DAG that passes immutable artifact identities into isolated Kubernetes task runtimes.

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.providers.cncf.kubernetes.operators.pod import KubernetesPodOperator
from datetime import datetime

with DAG(
    dag_id="versioned_rag_release",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    schedule=None,
    catchup=False,
    max_active_runs=1,
    tags=["mlops", "rag"],
) as dag:
    validate = KubernetesPodOperator(
        task_id="validate_sources",
        image=PIPELINE_IMAGE,
        cmds=["python", "-m", "pipeline.validate"],
        arguments=["--manifest", DATASET_MANIFEST],
    )
    embed = KubernetesPodOperator(
        task_id="build_embeddings",
        image=PIPELINE_IMAGE,
        cmds=["python", "-m", "pipeline.embed"],
        arguments=[
            "--manifest", DATASET_MANIFEST,
            "--embedding-version", EMBEDDING_VERSION,
            "--collection", COLLECTION_ID,
        ],
    )
    evaluate = KubernetesPodOperator(
        task_id="evaluate_retrieval",
        image=PIPELINE_IMAGE,
        cmds=["python", "-m", "pipeline.evaluate"],
        arguments=["--suite", EVAL_SUITE, "--candidate", COLLECTION_ID],
    )

    validate >> embed >> evaluate

Code walkthrough
DAG definition: The DAG object stores scheduling and concurrency policy; schedule=None makes release creation externally triggered.
Concurrency guard: max_active_runs=1 prevents overlapping candidate workflows from writing or evaluating the same candidate collection identity. This abbreviated DAG does not promote a production alias; a separate gated promotion task performs that state change.
Task runtime: Each KubernetesPodOperator launches domain work in the immutable pipeline image after DAG import.
Artifact handoff: Task arguments carry dataset, embedding, evaluation-suite, and candidate-collection identities. The embedding task writes its output at COLLECTION_ID; its completion manifest is the evidence that evaluation reads before accepting that collection.
Dependency state: The shift operators create validation → embedding → evaluation edges; Airflow records each task instance and attempt.
Result: The scheduler owns eligibility and task state, while isolated containers own validation, embedding, and evaluation work.
Limits: A production DAG still needs explicit output manifests, retries by failure class, secrets and service accounts, resource requests, timeouts, alerts, and a separate gated promotion task.


DAG-import rule
Import-time dataset downloads, GPU initialization, external API calls, and large namespace scans slow parsing and can make scheduler health depend on external systems.
The scheduler repeatedly parses DAG files. Expensive or unreliable import-time work slows the control plane and can make every DAG appear broken.

6.6 Safe re-execution and idempotent tasks
The example DAG can launch isolated tasks. Retries and historical runs will repeat code, so ambiguous partitions and irreversible side effects can duplicate or overwrite production state. Each run is bound to a logical data interval or immutable release identity, while computation and promotion remain separate.



Table 6.4: Re-execution is safe only when time, identity, and side effects are explicit.










Mechanism
Safe pattern
Failure to avoid




Retry
Attempt-scoped output, validation, then one committed generation
Appending duplicate rows or partially replacing a model


Backfill
The run’s logical interval and versioned upstream snapshot
Reading today’s mutable input for an old date


Catchup
Enable only when every historical interval is meaningful and resourced
Accidental flood of years of runs


Sensor / wait
Deferrable or event-driven waiting with timeout
Occupying a worker while polling indefinitely


External API
Idempotency key with persisted response identity
Duplicate billing, notification, or deployment


Promotion
Manual or policy gate updates an alias after validation
A retried compute task silently deploys






Retries distinguish transient infrastructure failures from deterministic code or data failures. Exponential backoff helps a temporary dependency recover; it does not fix a schema mismatch. After the retry budget, the task state, relevant logs, input identities, and responsible component remain visible without reconstructing the run from a terminal.

Worked calculation: retrying a partition task safely
Attempt 1: Partition 07 writes to an attempt-scoped path, loses its worker, and remains uncommitted.
Eligibility: The scheduler classifies the failure as transient and retries the same logical interval and input manifest.
Attempt 2: The task writes a new generation, validates row counts and hashes, and emits one completion record keyed by task, interval, and input identity.
Commit: A coordinator advances the manifest pointer exactly once; a late completion from Attempt 1 cannot overwrite the committed generation.
Conclusion: Attempt-scoped outputs and one publication step keep retries from duplicating or partially replacing state.

title: 7  Operating a grounded-answer system end to end
text:
7.1 Defining the end-to-end service target
How do all six layers cooperate when a production answer becomes less grounded even though the service remains available? The preceding chapters produced versioned artifacts, recoverable distributed jobs, serving bundles, evidence, durable and derived storage, and retryable pipelines. Those results form one system whose release guarantees connect an alert to a verified recovery.
The three panels connect grounded-answer inputs to coordinated release evidence, then to incident triage and the next improvement cycle.
Every technical layer is now available. An end-to-end design still needs a product definition that prevents teams from optimizing local metrics while breaking trust, privacy, or reproducibility. The workload, evidence responsibilities, and system guarantees define how the components fit together.
The case is a multi-tenant grounded-answer service. Users ask questions about a controlled document corpus. The system retrieves authorized passages, generates an answer, attaches citations, and records enough evidence to evaluate and replay the request without storing unnecessary sensitive content.
The retriever selects and authorizes evidence; the generator constructs an answer from that context; the evaluator checks claims and citations; and the release identity records the exact combination. A failure can therefore be localized without labeling every wrong answer as a model-weight defect.
Each system guarantee has a producing component, a machine-verifiable record, and a stop action. For example, the retrieval pipeline produces ACL-aware source identities, the trace records what was selected, and the release gate blocks a candidate whose negative-access tests fail. A guarantee without a stop action is only an aspiration.

7.3 Tracing documents from ingestion to retrieval
The identity graph defines the required connections. The first active path turns controlled documents into searchable state without losing source, access, deletion, or version information. Committed generations and quality checks make the ingestion path reproducible.

Source snapshot. Source object versions and authorization metadata form an immutable corpus manifest.
Validation. MIME type, decoding, duplication, required metadata, malware and policy rules, and document counts are checked.
Chunking. A versioned splitter produces chunk-to-source offsets, text hashes, ordering, and inherited access controls.
Embedding. One immutable model revision, preprocessing rule, dimension, and normalization choice produces the vectors.
Index build. The configured ANN structure is written to a candidate collection while the production alias remains unchanged.
Reconciliation. Expected and actual counts, unique IDs, deletes, hashes, and per-tenant coverage are compared.
Evaluation. Retrieval cases, filtered queries, freshness tests, latency load, and failure recovery test the candidate.

text:
7.7 Finding the cause of a groundedness incident
The evidence path spans every component. The incident begins with an available service whose answers for newly added policy documents become less grounded. An ordered investigation localizes the failing artifact or stage before any component is blamed.

Case status
This illustrative incident follows an incomplete corpus release from detection to recovery. Its figures are example values, not observations from a production deployment.


Worked calculation: quality regression after a corpus release
Production change: Release r218 keeps serving bundle b12.4 but moves retrieval alias from collection c40-e3-i7 to c41-e3-i7.
Alert: The sampled groundedness rate falls from 0.91 to 0.78 for the new-policy slice; HTTP errors and TTFT remain within objective.
Trace evidence: Failed answers have low retrieval scores and omit source IDs introduced in corpus generation 41.
Lineage check: The corpus manifest expects 12.0 million chunks, but the committed collection contains 11.2 million; one tenant partition is absent.
Pipeline evidence: An embedding task retried after a worker loss. Its wrapper treated process exit zero as success and did not reconcile per-partition counts before promotion.
Immediate mitigation: The retrieval alias returns to c40-e3-i7, bundle b12.4 remains in place, affected owners receive notification, and failed traces remain preserved.
Repaired candidate: A new candidate contains the rebuilt partition, reconciled counts and hashes, authorization/retrieval/freshness results, and shadow and canary evidence.
Prevention: Completion-manifest reconciliation becomes a hard task gate, and compute tasks no longer change aliases.
Conclusion: The service was operationally healthy but semantically degraded; joined release, trace, storage, and pipeline evidence isolated an incomplete derived artifact.

Strong: expected/actual count mismatch and missing partition IDs align with failed cases.

section: 7.8 Regression prevention with evaluation gates
text:
7.8 Regression prevention with evaluation gates
Rollback restores user-facing quality. Rebuilding one missing partition fixes this generation but leaves the pipeline capable of promoting another incomplete collection. A prevention control at the visibility point stops another invalid collection from reaching live traffic.

Machine-verifiable guarantee. The expected partition set, row count ranges, unique-ID constraints, vector dimensions, ACL coverage, and delete reconciliation are expressed as checks.
Promotion separation. The compute DAG writes only candidate generations; a separate gated task updates the production alias.
Validated success. The task succeeds only after validation artifacts are committed, rather than when a worker merely exits zero.
Regression slice. Failed requests and nearby cases become a versioned new-policy evaluation slice.
Recovery test. A deliberately missing partition confirms that publication remains blocked and the old alias stays live.
Coverage signals. Expected-versus-searchable count, per-partition freshness, and alias target changes become alert signals.
Post-release evidence. Shadow and then canary traffic carry the same groundedness and retrieval measurements through the evidence window.


Control-placement principle
The preventive gate belongs at the point where invalid state could become visible.
A dashboard can detect a bad collection after promotion; a commit manifest and promotion check keep the invalid collection away from live traffic.

A.1 Measurement details
A quantitative result is meaningful only when its workload, aggregation window, and version context are known. The relationships cover cost, capacity, memory, synchronization, latency, evaluation, storage, retrieval, and pipeline duration. Their values support comparison and diagnosis while the surrounding evidence explains each production decision.
Comparisons depend on population, aggregation window, and version context. Mean request latency and p99 latency answer different questions; the relevant-precision GPU peak differs from a nominal peak; retrieval scores change across embedding spaces; and throughput changes with workload shape.
The equations provide compact relationships. A metric remains ambiguous when its population, aggregation, scale, exclusions, or version context is missing. The following details make a dashboard or benchmark interpretable.

title: Appendix B — MLOps glossary
text:
MLOps combines vocabulary from infrastructure, distributed systems, model evaluation, storage, retrieval, and orchestration. The same term can connect several components, so each definition names the object, behavior, or measurement involved. The entries use consistent meanings across training, serving, evaluation, storage, and pipelines.
Access pattern. The measurable read/write, size, concurrency, sharing, durability, latency, and lifecycle behavior of data.
Agent trajectory. The ordered model, reasoning-state, tool-call, observation, and state-transition path taken by an agent.
All-reduce. A collective that combines values from all ranks and returns the result to every rank.
ANN. Approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval that prunes the search space instead of comparing every vector.
Artifact. A versionable product of a run, such as a checkpoint, dataset manifest, image, metric report, or index.
Backfill. Execution of a pipeline for historical logical intervals or previously unprocessed partitions.
Batching. Combining multiple items or requests so one compute operation uses hardware more efficiently.
Blue/green deployment. A release pattern that keeps stable and candidate environments available for a controlled traffic switch.
Canary. A candidate release exposed to a small controlled share of live traffic before wider promotion.
Checkpoint. A saved state sufficient to resume a computation under stated compatibility conditions.
Chunk. A bounded source segment used as one embedding and retrieval unit, with links back to its source.
Cold start. Latency and failure risk incurred when a service creates capacity and loads runtime/model state before serving.
Collective. A coordinated communication operation involving a defined group of distributed ranks.
Consistency (evaluator). The fraction of repeated judgments that agree with the modal label for one unchanged case.
Context parallelism. Distribution of long sequence context across devices to reduce per-device memory or computation.
Control plane. The component that stores desired state and reconciles deployments, capacity, configuration, and rollout actions.
Critical path. The longest dependency path whose summed duration lower-bounds a DAG’s completion time.
Data drift. A change in the production input distribution relative to a reference distribution.
Data parallelism. Replicated computation over distinct input shards with synchronized model updates.
DAG. A directed acyclic graph representing tasks and prerequisite relationships.
DDP. PyTorch’s replicated-model distributed data-parallel implementation with gradient synchronization.
Decode. Autoregressive generation after prefill, usually one next-token step per active sequence.
Disaggregated serving. Separation of serving stages such as prefill and decode into independently scheduled capacity.
Distributed sampler. A deterministic policy that partitions dataset examples among data-parallel ranks.
Embedding. A model-produced fixed-length numeric representation used to compare items in a vector space.
Evaluator. A deterministic rule, model, or human protocol that maps system evidence to a quality judgment.
Experiment run. One traceable execution with recorded parameters, code, inputs, outputs, metrics, and environment.
Expert parallelism. Distribution of mixture-of-experts components and token routing across devices.
F1 score. The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
FSDP. Fully Sharded Data Parallel, which shards selected model, gradient, and optimizer state across ranks.
Gang scheduling. Admission of all resources required by a coordinated distributed job as one placement decision.
Groundedness. The extent to which an answer’s material claims are supported by the supplied evidence.
HNSW. A layered proximity-graph ANN index with tunable construction and search effort.
Hybrid retrieval. Combination of dense, sparse, metadata, and optional reranking stages.
Idempotency. The property that safe repeated execution has the same externally visible result as one execution.
Inference engine. The runtime that schedules model forward passes, manages memory/KV state, and emits generated tokens.
Inter-token latency. Elapsed time between successive generated tokens during decode.
IOPS. Completed storage input/output operations per second for a stated operation shape.
IVF. An inverted-file ANN method that searches selected coarse vector partitions.
KV cache. Stored attention keys and values reused across autoregressive decode steps.
Lineage. The recorded graph connecting outputs to exact inputs, code, configuration, environment, and producer run.
Log. A discrete timestamped event record with structured diagnostic context.
Metric. A numeric time series aggregated over events or measurements.
MFU. Model FLOPs Utilization: observed model arithmetic rate divided by relevant hardware peak.
Model registry. A controlled store of immutable model versions, their training-run links, metadata, and promotion state.
NCCL. NVIDIA’s communication library implementing GPU-oriented collective operations.
Object storage. API-addressed storage for objects identified by keys, with behavior distinct from a POSIX file system.
OpenTelemetry. An open standard and SDK/protocol family for traces, metrics, and logs.
Pipeline parallelism. Distribution of consecutive model layers across stages that exchange activations and gradients.
Prediction drift. A change in the distribution of model outputs relative to a reference.
Prefill. Parallel processing of input prompt tokens to create the initial KV state.
Prompt decision tree. An explicit ordered representation of evaluator decisions, overrides, and terminal verdicts.
Quantization. Representation of weights, activations, or cache values with reduced numerical precision.
Rank. One process identity in a distributed process group; global and local ranks serve different scopes.
Recall@k. The fraction of relevant reference items found among the top-k retrieved results.
Recovery Point Objective. The maximum acceptable amount of work or data lost after failure.
Recovery Time Objective. The target time to restore an acceptable level of service or computation.
Rendezvous. The discovery and coordination mechanism through which distributed ranks form a process group.
Reranker. A more expensive scorer applied to a reduced candidate set to improve final ordering.
Serving bundle. The immutable weights, tokenizer, engine image, configuration, compatibility, and release metadata deployed together.
Service Level Objective. A measurable target for service behavior over a defined population and time window.
Speculative decoding. Generation that proposes tokens with a draft model and verifies them with the target model.
Tensor parallelism. Distribution of tensor operations within a model layer across devices.
Time to First Token. Elapsed time from request admission to the first generated token.
Trace. A causally ordered set of spans describing one operation across components.
Vector database. A stateful service that stores vector records and metadata and supports similarity-oriented retrieval.
World size. The number of processes participating in a distributed process group.
